prompt: Charges of $+4.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ sit at two vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $0.10\ \mathrm m$. A $+2.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ charge sits at the third vertex. Find the magnitude of the net force on it, in N. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

why: divided by $\cos30^\circ$ instead of multiplying the sum
treated the two forces as perpendicular

rubric.text: Each pair force from Coulomb's law
Components: parts along the base cancel, parts along the symmetry axis add

solution:
Each repulsion: $F=kq_1q_2/a^2=7.19\ \mathrm N$ (coulomb).
Each force points away from its source, $30^\circ$ from the symmetry axis (vec-comp).
Components along the base cancel by symmetry.
Components along the symmetry axis add: $2F\cos30^\circ=12.5\ \mathrm N$.
hints: Split each force along and across the symmetry axis.

prompt: Point charges $+9.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ at $x=0$ and $-1.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ at $x=0.20\ \mathrm m$ lie on the $x$-axis. At what finite $x$ in metres on the axis does the net field vanish?

why: used $x=3d$ from the square root alone

rubric.text: Locate the region: must be outside the pair, beyond the smaller charge

solution:
Between the charges both fields point the same way, so no zero there (coulomb).
Beyond the larger charge the larger field always wins, so the zero is past the $-1\ \mu$C charge (vec-comp: directions).
Set $9/x^2=1/(x-0.20)^2$, so $3(x-0.20)=x$.
$x=0.30\ \mathrm m$.
hints: Which side of the weaker charge can the fields cancel on?

prompt: A solid insulating sphere of radius $R$ has charge density $\rho=\rho_0\,r/R$ for $r\le R$. Find the ratio $E(R/2)\,/\,E(3R)$ of field magnitudes.

why: treated the density as uniform: $E\propto r$ inside, $E(R/2)/E(3R)=9/2$
used the full charge at $R/2$ (ignored the enclosed fraction)
used the ratio of radii only

rubric.text: Enclosed charge by integrating $\rho\,4\pi r^2dr$: $Q(r)\propto r^4$

solution:
Gauss with spherical symmetry (gauss): $E=kQ_{enc}/r^2$.
Inside, $Q_{enc}=\int_0^r\rho_0\frac{r'}{R}4\pi r'^2dr'=\pi\rho_0r^4/R$, so $E(R/2)=\rho_0R/(16\varepsilon_0)$.
Outside, $Q=\pi\rho_0R^3$, so $E(3R)=\rho_0R/(36\varepsilon_0)$ (scaling).
Ratio $=36/16=9/4$.
hints: Find Q_enc(r) with an integral, not r cubed.

prompt: A very long solid insulating cylinder of radius $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ carries uniform volume charge density $3.0\ \mu\mathrm{C/m^3}$. Find the field magnitude $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the axis, in V/m. $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$

rubric.text: Gauss on a coaxial cylinder: $E=\lambda/(2\pi\varepsilon_0 r)$
Numerical value with consistent SI units

solution:
Per unit length the cylinder holds $\lambda=\rho\pi R^2$ (gauss, units: convert $\mu$C and cm).
A coaxial Gaussian cylinder of radius $r>R$ gives $E\,2\pi r=\lambda/\varepsilon_0$.
$E=\rho R^2/(2\varepsilon_0r)=1.36\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{V/m}$.
hints: Outside, only the enclosed charge per length matters.

prompt: Three point charges $+2.0\ \mu\mathrm C$, $+2.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ and $-4.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ sit at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side $0.30\ \mathrm m$. Find the energy in J needed to pull them all apart to infinite separation. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

rubric.text: Total energy is a sum over pairs, each counted once
Sign of each pair term from the charge product
Energy needed is minus the total $U$

solution:
$U=k\sum_{pairs}q_iq_j/a$ (potential energy of a charge set; each pair once).
Pairs: $(2)(2)+2\,(2)(-4)=4-16=-12$ in $\mu\mathrm C^2$ (coulomb signs).
$U=-8.99\times10^{9}\cdot12\times10^{-12}/0.30=-0.36\ \mathrm J$.
Separating to infinity costs $+0.36\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Count three pairs, signs matter.

prompt: A thin ring of radius $0.30\ \mathrm m$ carries uniform charge $+5.0\ \mu\mathrm C$. A $1.0\ \mathrm g$ bead with charge $+2.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ is released from rest on the ring's axis, $0.40\ \mathrm m$ from the centre. Ignoring gravity, find its speed far away, in m/s. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

rubric.text: Axial potential $V=kQ/\sqrt{R^2+x^2}$ by superposition of ring elements
Mass in kg and numerical value

solution:
Every ring element is $\sqrt{R^2+x^2}=0.50\ \mathrm m$ away, so $V=kQ/0.50=8.99\times10^{4}\ \mathrm V$ (potential).
The bead gains $qV=0.180\ \mathrm J$ going to $V=0$ (work-energy).
$v=\sqrt{2qV/m}=19\ \mathrm{m/s}$ with $m=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kg}$.
hints: Potential is a scalar sum, no vector components needed.

prompt: Point charges $+1.0\ \mathrm{nC}$, $-2.0\ \mathrm{nC}$, $+1.0\ \mathrm{nC}$ lie on a line, spaced $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart with the middle one at the origin. Find the potential in V at $1.0\ \mathrm m$ from the origin on the line. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

why: factor 4 from counting both outer charges twice
assumed zero because the net charge is zero

rubric.text: Net charge and dipole moment vanish: leading term is the quadrupole

solution:
Net charge $0$, dipole moment $0$ by symmetry, so the monopole and dipole terms drop (multipole).
Expand $kq[1/(r-a)-2/r+1/(r+a)]$ with $a/r\ll1$ (small-angle expansion).
Linear terms cancel; second order leaves $2kqa^2/r^3$.
$V=2(8.99\times10^{9})(10^{-9})(10^{-2})^2=1.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm V$.
hints: Expand each term in a/r; what survives?

prompt: A small dipole of moment $p=2.0\ \mathrm{nC\,m}$ lies along the line to a fixed point charge $Q=3.0\ \mathrm{nC}$, $0.10\ \mathrm m$ away, and points along the line. Find the force magnitude on the dipole in N. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

why: derivative of $1/r^2$ taken as $1/r^3$ without the 2

rubric.text: Uniform-field idea fails: force needs the field gradient

solution:
In a uniform field the net force is zero, so only the gradient of $E$ matters (multipole).
$E=kQ/r^2$ gives $|dE/dr|=2kQ/r^3$ (rates of change).
$F=p\cdot2kQ/r^3$ (Coulomb field of $Q$).
$=2(8.99\times10^{9})(3\times10^{-9})(2\times10^{-9})/10^{-3}=1.08\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm N$.
hints: Differentiate the field of Q along the line.

prompt: A conducting spherical shell, inner radius $0.10\ \mathrm m$ and outer radius $0.20\ \mathrm m$, carries net charge $-2.0\ \mathrm{nC}$. A $+6.0\ \mathrm{nC}$ point charge sits at its centre. Find the surface charge density magnitude on the outer surface, in $\mathrm{C/m^2}$.

why: used the point charge alone on the outer surface
used the shell's net charge, ignoring induction
gave the inner-surface charge on the outer surface (wrong radius)

rubric.text: Field inside conductor is zero: inner surface carries $-6$ nC (Gauss)
Charge conservation: outer surface carries $-2-(-6)=+4$ nC

solution:
Gaussian sphere inside the metal: $E=0$, so the inner surface holds $-6.0\ \mathrm{nC}$ (conductors, gauss).
Shell net charge is $-2.0$ nC, so the outer surface holds $-2.0-(-6.0)=+4.0\ \mathrm{nC}$.
$\sigma=4.0\times10^{-9}/(4\pi\,0.20^2)=7.96\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}$.
hints: What must the inner surface hold for E to vanish in the metal?

prompt: Two conducting spheres of radii $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $6.0\ \mathrm{cm}$, far apart, are joined by a thin wire and hold a total charge of $8.0\ \mathrm{nC}$. Find the field magnitude at the surface of the smaller sphere, in V/m. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

why: gave the field of the larger sphere
assigned the larger charge to the small sphere
put the whole charge on the small sphere

solution:
The wire makes one equipotential, so $q_1/R_1=q_2/R_2$ (conductors, potential).
With $q_1+q_2=8$ nC and $R_2=3R_1$: $q_1=2.0$ nC.
Field at the surface of the small sphere: $E=kq_1/R_1^2=8.99\times10^{9}(2\times10^{-9})/(4\times10^{-4})=4.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/m}$.
hints: Equal potential, not equal charge.

prompt: A point charge $q=2.0\ \mathrm{nC}$ is $0.10\ \mathrm m$ above a large grounded conducting plane. Find the work in J an external agent must do to move it slowly to infinity. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$

why: used the full two-charge energy at separation $2d$
gave the force instead of the work

rubric.text: Do not use the full pair energy: field exists on one side only

solution:
Replace the plane by an image $-q$ a distance $d'$ below it (images).
At height $d'$ the force is $kq^2/(2d')^2$ (attractive).
Work: $W=\int_d^\infty kq^2/(4d'^2)\,dd'=kq^2/(4d)$ (work-energy).
$=8.99\times10^{9}(4\times10^{-18})/0.40=9.0\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Integrate the image force; only half the pair energy.

prompt: A point charge $5.0\ \mathrm{nC}$ is $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ above a large grounded conducting plane. Find the magnitude of the induced surface charge density, in $\mathrm{C/m^2}$, at the point of the plane $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ from the foot of the perpendicular.

rubric.text: Image charge $-q$ at depth $h$ replaces the plane
Normal field at the plane from charge plus image: $E_n=2kqh/(h^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}$

solution:
Image $-q$ at depth $h$ gives the right field above the plane (images).
At in-plane distance $\rho$ the tangential parts cancel and the normal parts add: $E_n=2kqh/(h^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}$ (coulomb).
Boundary condition for a conductor: $\sigma=\varepsilon_0E_n=qh/[2\pi(h^2+\rho^2)^{3/2}]$ (conductors).
With $h=\rho=0.05$: $\sigma=1.13\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{C/m^2}$.
hints: σ equals ε0 times the normal field at the surface.

prompt: Two concentric conducting spheres have radii $5.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ (held at $100\ \mathrm V$) and $10\ \mathrm{cm}$ (grounded). There is no charge between them. Find the potential in V at $7.5\ \mathrm{cm}$.

why: used $1/r^2$ (the field's form) for the potential

solution:
Laplace with spherical symmetry (laplace): $V=A/r+B$.
Boundary values: $V(0.05)=100$, $V(0.10)=0$.
$V(r)=100\,\dfrac{1/r-1/0.10}{1/0.05-1/0.10}$ (potential).
At $r=0.075$: $100\cdot(13.33-10)/10=33.3\ \mathrm V$.
hints: Not linear in r: solve ∇²V=0 for r-only dependence.

prompt: A hollow cube has no charge inside. Its six faces are held at $120,\ 60,\ 0,\ 0,\ 30$ and $30\ \mathrm V$ (each face uniform; treat the gaps at the edges as negligible). Find the potential in V at the cube's centre.

why: used a mean-value factor for eight faces

rubric.text: Symmetry: each face acting alone gives the same centre value
Sum is $V_{face}/6$ per face: average of six faces

solution:
Inside the cube $\nabla^2V=0$ and the boundary data fix $V$ uniquely (laplace).
Split into six problems with one face at its value, the rest at 0 (superposition).
By cube symmetry each contributes the same fraction, and a uniform $V_0$ on all six gives $V_0$ at the centre, so the fraction is $1/6$.
$V=(120+60+0+0+30+30)/6=40\ \mathrm V$.
hints: Equal-weight averaging needs how many faces?

prompt: A $12\ \mathrm V$ battery is connected across a $6.0\ \mu\mathrm F$ capacitor in series with a parallel pair of $3.0\ \mu\mathrm F$ and $6.0\ \mu\mathrm F$ capacitors, all initially uncharged. Find the energy stored in the $3.0\ \mu\mathrm F$ capacitor, in J.

rubric.text: Parallel pair equivalent $9.0\ \mu$F; series pair shares equal charge

solution:
Parallel pair: $C_p=3+6=9\ \mu\mathrm F$ (capacitors).
Series elements carry equal charge, so voltage splits inversely to $C$ (series reduction): $V_p=12\cdot6/(6+9)=4.8\ \mathrm V$.
The $3.0\ \mu$F capacitor sees the full $V_p$.
$U=\tfrac12(3\times10^{-6})(4.8)^2=3.46\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Equal charge on series elements; voltage splits inversely to C.

prompt: A $2.0\ \mathrm{nF}$ parallel-plate capacitor is charged to $100\ \mathrm V$ and then disconnected. Its plates are slowly pulled apart from separation $d$ to $3d$. Find the work in J done by the external agent.

why: held $V$ fixed: $U\propto1/d$, magnitude of the change
gave the final energy, not the change

solution:
Disconnected means $Q$ is constant (capacitors).
$U=Q^2/2C$ and $C\propto1/d$, so $U\propto d$.
$U_0=\tfrac12CV^2=1.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm J$; at $3d$, $U=3U_0$.
Work-energy: $W=\Delta U=2U_0=2.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Which quantity stays fixed after disconnecting?

prompt: A $5.0\ \mathrm{nF}$ parallel-plate capacitor charged to $200\ \mathrm V$ is isolated. A slab with $\kappa=4$ is then slid in until it fills the gap. Find the energy in J given up by the stored field as the slab enters.
solution:
No battery, so $Q$ stays fixed (capacitors).
Filling with dielectric: $C\to4C$ and $U=Q^2/2C\to U_0/4$ (dielectrics).
$U_0=\tfrac12(5\times10^{-9})(200)^2=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm J$.
Energy released $=U_0(1-\tfrac14)=7.5\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm J$ (work-energy: pulled in by the field).
hints: Fixed Q: does U go up or down?

prompt: An air capacitor has $C_0=3.0\ \mathrm{pF}$. A slab with $\kappa=5$, full plate area and thickness equal to half the gap, is placed flat against one plate. Find the new capacitance in pF.

why: treated the layers as side by side (parallel)

rubric.text: Slab and air gap are in series

solution:
The layers are stacked across the field, so they are in series (dielectrics).
Slab: $C_1=\kappa\varepsilon_0A/(d/2)=2\kappa C_0$; air: $C_2=2C_0$.
$C=\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}=C_0\dfrac{2\kappa}{\kappa+1}$ (capacitors, series).
$=3.0\cdot10/6=5.0\ \mathrm{pF}$.
hints: Layers stacked along the field add as series capacitors.

prompt: An ideal $6.0\ \mathrm V$ battery is in series with a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor and then a parallel pair of $3.0\ \Omega$ and $6.0\ \Omega$. Find the power in W dissipated in the $6.0\ \Omega$ resistor.

why: used the total current in the $6\ \Omega$
split the current equally between the branches
used the battery voltage across it

rubric.text: Reduce the parallel pair to $2.0\ \Omega$, total $4.0\ \Omega$

solution:
Parallel pair: $3\cdot6/9=2.0\ \Omega$; total $4.0\ \Omega$ (dc-circuits).
$I=6/4=1.5\ \mathrm A$; pair voltage $=1.5\cdot2=3.0\ \mathrm V$ (potential drop).
The $6\ \Omega$ resistor sees the full pair voltage: $P=V^2/R=9/6=1.5\ \mathrm W$.
hints: Find the voltage across the pair first.

prompt: An infinite ladder repeats one stage: a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor in series along the rail, then a $2.0\ \Omega$ resistor across the rails. A $10\ \mathrm V$ battery drives the input. Find the battery current in A.

rubric.text: Self-similarity: adding a stage leaves $R_{eq}$ unchanged

solution:
Removing one stage leaves an identical infinite ladder, so $R_{eq}=x$ is unchanged (scaling).
One stage: series $2$, then parallel of $2$ with $x$: $x=2+\dfrac{2x}{2+x}$ (dc-circuits).
$x^2-2x-4=0$, so $x=1+\sqrt5=3.24\ \Omega$.
$I=10/3.24=3.09\ \mathrm A$.
hints: Add one stage in front and demand the same resistance.

prompt: Three branches connect a top wire to a bottom wire. Left: a $12\ \mathrm V$ battery (positive terminal up) in series with $4.0\ \Omega$. Middle: $3.0\ \Omega$. Right: a $6.0\ \mathrm V$ battery (positive terminal up) in series with $2.0\ \Omega$. Find the current through the middle resistor, in A.

rubric.text: Loop rule on left and middle
Loop rule on right and middle

solution:
Let $V$ be the top-minus-bottom voltage (kirchhoff junction rule).
Left current $(12-V)/4$, right $(6-V)/2$, middle $V/3$.
Junction: $(12-V)/4+(6-V)/2=V/3$, so $72=13V$ and $V=72/13\ \mathrm V$ (loop rules).
$I_{mid}=V/3=24/13=1.85\ \mathrm A$.
hints: Use the common voltage between top and bottom as the unknown.

prompt: Three branches connect a top wire to a bottom wire. Left: a $12\ \mathrm V$ battery (positive terminal up) in series with $4.0\ \Omega$. Middle: $3.0\ \Omega$. Right: a $9.0\ \mathrm V$ battery with its positive terminal down, in series with $2.0\ \Omega$. Find the magnitude of the current through the middle resistor, in A.

rubric.text: Junction rule with signed branch currents
Right-branch EMF enters with a minus sign
Solve for the common node voltage

solution:
Let $V$ be top-minus-bottom (kirchhoff). Left: $(12-V)/4$. Right: $(-9-V)/2$ because its EMF opposes. Middle: $V/3$.
Junction rule: $(12-V)/4+(-9-V)/2=V/3$, so $-18=13V$ (dc-circuits).
$V=-18/13\ \mathrm V$, so the middle current is $6/13=0.46\ \mathrm A$, flowing upward.
hints: Flip the sign of the right EMF; the node voltage may come out negative.

prompt: A $5.0\ \mu\mathrm F$ capacitor, initially uncharged, charges through a $200\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor from a battery. Find the time in s at which the stored energy reaches half of its final value.
solution:
$\tau=RC=1.0\ \mathrm s$ (rc-transient).
$U=\tfrac12CV^2$ is proportional to $V^2$ (em-energy), so half energy means $V=V_0/\sqrt2$.
$1-e^{-t/\tau}=0.707$, so $t=-\tau\ln(0.293)$.
$t=1.23\ \mathrm s$.
hints: Energy goes as V squared, so V is not half.

prompt: A $10\ \mu\mathrm F$ capacitor charged to $100\ \mathrm V$ discharges through a $2.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor in series with a parallel pair of $6.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$. Find the total heat in J produced in the $3.0\ \mathrm{k\Omega}$ resistor.

rubric.text: All stored energy $\tfrac12CV^2=0.050$ J ends as heat
Pair resistance $2$ k$\Omega$: half of the series power
Within the pair, power $\propto1/R$: $3$ k$\Omega$ gets $2/3$

solution:
All the stored energy is dissipated: $\tfrac12CV^2=0.050\ \mathrm J$ (rc-transient; the decay rate drops out).
Series current is common, power $\propto R$ (dc-circuits): the pair ($2$ k$\Omega$ equivalent) gets $2/4=1/2$.
In the pair the voltage is common, power $\propto1/R$: the $3$ k$\Omega$ share is $2/3$.
Heat $=0.050\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac23=1.67\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm J$.
hints: Time constant is irrelevant to the total heat.

prompt: A copper wire of radius $1.0\ \mathrm{mm}$ carries $5.0\ \mathrm A$. The free-electron density is $8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ and $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$. How many seconds does an electron take to drift $1.0\ \mathrm m$ along the wire?

why: used the diameter as the radius

solution:
$I=nqAv_d$ (drude), so $v_d=I/(nq\pi r^2)$.
$A=\pi(10^{-3})^2=3.14\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ (units in metres).
$v_d=5/(8.5\times10^{28}\cdot1.6\times10^{-19}\cdot3.14\times10^{-6})=1.17\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.
$t=1/v_d=8.5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm s$, about $2.4$ hours.
hints: Drift is slow: use I = n q A v.

prompt: Copper has resistivity $1.70\times10^{-8}\ \Omega\,\mathrm m$ and free-electron density $8.5\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$. Use the Drude model with $q=1.60\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm C$ and $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$ to find the mean time between collisions, in s.
solution:
Drude: $\sigma=nq^2\tau/m_e$ (drude), with $\sigma=1/\rho$.
Solve $\tau=m_e/(nq^2\rho)$ (dimensions check: kg/(m$^{-3}$C$^2\,\Omega$m) gives s).
$\tau=\dfrac{9.11\times10^{-31}}{(8.5\times10^{28})(2.56\times10^{-38})(1.7\times10^{-8})}=2.5\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm s$.
hints: Resistivity is the inverse of the Drude conductivity.

prompt: A uniformly charged insulating sphere of radius $0.10\ \mathrm m$ holds $2.0\ \mu\mathrm C$ of charge. Find the total electrostatic field energy in J, inside and outside. $k=8.99\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/C^2}$
solution:
Gauss gives the field everywhere (gauss).
Outside, energy density $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ integrates to $kQ^2/2R$ (em-energy).
Inside, $E\propto r$ integrates to $kQ^2/10R$.
Total $=\tfrac35kQ^2/R=0.6(8.99\times10^{9})(4\times10^{-12})/0.10=0.216\ \mathrm J$.
hints: The field inside also stores energy.

prompt: Parallel plates of area $0.040\ \mathrm m^2$ in air have uniform field $1.0\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ between them (negligible outside). Find the attractive force in N between the plates. $\varepsilon_0=8.85\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$

why: used the full field $E$ on the plate charge
area slip, a factor of ten

rubric.text: Energy density $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ and energy per volume
Do not use $\sigma A E$: the plate's own field is $E/2$

solution:
Field energy density is $u=\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$ (em-energy).
Opening the gap by $dx$ at fixed charge adds energy $uA\,dx$, so $F=uA$ (capacitors).
$F=\tfrac12(8.85\times10^{-12})(10^{10})(0.040)=1.77\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm N$.
Equivalent: one plate's charge $\sigma A$ in the other plate's field $E/2$.
hints: One plate feels only the other plate's field.
